text:
maia: quick check — we've been seeing intermittent "unexpected end of JSON input" errors in the Go SDK when streaming high-throughput SSE. Repro only under load. any ideas?

alex_w: seen that before. usually SSE frames get split across TCP chunks and our parser assumes full event payload per chunk. first guess: we're attempting to json.Unmarshal on partial data.

chip: +1. also watch for the "data: " prefix lines. If you just feed raw chunks into the decoder you'll get partial JSONs. need to frame by event boundary (blank line) and then parse the assembled data.

maia: we're collecting lines and joining until blank line, but still see cases where multiple events arrive glued together or a single event split across many small chunks. under heavy load this queues up and goroutines pile up — seems like backpressure issue.

nina: are we using bufio.Reader.ReadBytes('\n') or something? ReadBytes can be expensive on tiny fragments. what does the Go client read loop look like?

maia: currently:
```
for {
  n, err := resp.Body.Read(buf)
  if n>0 { handleChunk(buf[:n]) }
  if err!=nil { break }
}
```
handleChunk naively appends to a bytes.Buffer and tries to parse whenever it contains a "}". messy.

alex_w: that's the core issue. heuristics like searching for '}' are brittle. better approach: implement an event assembly state machine: accumulate until you hit the event delimiter ("\n\n") then process event block. also enforce max event size and backpressure (drop or reject) instead of unbounded buffering.

chip: concrete suggestions:
- use a small ring buffer or bounded byte.Buffer to avoid OOM/goroutine growth
- parse lines: only lines starting with "data:" are payload lines, ignore others
- handle chunk concatenation: one chunk may contain 2+ events, so loop draining events from buffer until none left
- when buffer exceeds threshold (e.g., 1MB), increment a metric and either stall reader or close connection depending on policy

maia: how do we stall the reader in Go without busy-looping?

nina: use a semaphore that limits number of in-flight events being processed. In read loop, after appending data check if semaphore permits process; if not, pause by blocking on the semaphore (which will naturally apply backpressure because Read will block when app isn't reading?). be careful: resp.Body.Read will continue to supply data from OS to kernel buffers; you want to stop processing to allow kernel buffers to fill and upstream to slow down. blocking the goroutine that reads from resp.Body is fine — kernel space will handle the rest.

alex_w: another option is to use io.Pipe between the network reader and parser with limited buffer sizes, so the network reader will block when pipe is full. but simpler: keep single reader goroutine that only does minimal framing work and pushes framed events into a bounded channel. workers consume channel. if channel is full, reader blocks on send — that's natural backpressure.

maia: got it. bounded channel + single reader framing logic. how do we handle partial JSON inside the event "data:" lines — some events are ndjson (multiple JSON objects separated by '\n') and some are large nested JSONs split across multiple event lines.

chip: recommended parse flow:
1) assemble event text (concat all data: lines with '\n') until blank line end
2) if Content-Type or first token indicates ndjson, split by '\n' and decode each line as an independent JSON
3) otherwise, treat as single JSON blob — decode with json.Decoder on a bytes.Reader so decoder errors are explicit
4) always cap decoder input size and catch io.ErrUnexpectedEOF to detect truncation; on truncation, treat as malformed and increment metric (or request reconnect)

nina: for ndjson you can also stream-decode by creating a bufio.Scanner over the assembled body and scanning lines. scanner has max token size config (Scanner.Buffer) to avoid DoS from huge lines.

maia: any cross-language tips? we have Node and Kotlin clients also hitting similar problems.

alex_w: Node: use the eventsource-like parsing where you buffer per-event. For native fetch streaming, use a TextDecoder and iterate over chunks, append to a string buffer, then split on "\n\n" for events. Respect backpressure by pausing stream consumption: the Streams API has read() and controller.enqueue semantics. If you're using a high-level EventSource polyfill, ensure you set an appropriate highWaterMark on the underlying stream.

chip: Kotlin/OkHttp: OkHttp's source.readUtf8LineStrict will throw if a line exceeds limit. Use readUtf8Line with safe behaviour and a bounded buffer. Also prefer Flow/Coroutine channels with limited capacity to avoid spawning coroutines per incoming chunk.

maia: thanks. any quick code snippet for Go reader->frame->bounded channel pattern?

alex_w: quick sketch:
```
framer := make(chan string, 256) // bounded
go func(){
  var buf bytes.Buffer
  for {
    n, _ := r.Read(tmp)
    if n>0 { buf.Write(tmp[:n]) }
    for {
      idx := bytes.Index(buf.Bytes(), []byte("\n\n"))
      if idx==-1 { break }
      evt := buf.Next(idx+2)
      framer <- string(evt) // blocks when channel full
    }
    if err!=nil { break }
  }
  close(framer)
}()
// consumer workers read from framer
```
This blocks the framer send, which is desired backpressure. also guard evt size before sending.

chip: also add a per-connection metric for "framer_drops" and an alert if > X/min. helps detect clients pushing too fast.

maia: concrete next steps I will take:
- change Go SDK to single reader + bounded channel framer
- add scanner with max token size for lines
- add metrics for buffer growth and framer drops
- create a small load repro and run against runtime to confirm fix
I'll open a PR by EOD.

devex-bot: noted — adding follow-up task to #devex backlog: "Go SDK: bounded framer + backpressure for SSE".

ingest-bot: FYI — ingestion service saw spikes matching these timestamps; correlated with client reconnects.

maia: awesome, thanks everyone. pinging when PR's up for quick review. :thumbsup:

alex_w: happy to review. if you want I can add a simple Node repro too so we can test cross-client behavior. :eyes:

maia: please do. that would be helpful.

chip: one last note — be careful with keepalive/heartbeat. if you shut down connections aggressively you can trigger reconnection storms. implement exponential backoff and jitter on reconnects.

maia: noted. I'll include reconnect jitter in PR doc.

nina: if you want, add a small test harness that feeds fragmented event frames (random split positions) to the framer to validate correctness deterministically.

maia: will do, thanks!
